paragraphs: What is worth exploring is helping a learner understand a specific problem, not just producing the right answer for them. Observe whether you can listen to their reasoning, verify the teaching materials, design prompts, and accept that teaching plans need repeated revision.

First verify the learner's age, course content, organization, and local rules. Out-of-school academic tutoring for minors involves approval and practitioner requirements; using the names “tutoring”, one-on-one, or after-school care does not automatically exempt you from regulation.

This occupation corresponds to O*NET25-3041.00 and provides individual or small-group academic tutoring that supports formal courses or exam preparation. School classroom teaching, adult basic education, self-improvement courses, and university teaching assistants should be compared by their different duties.

Use the fictional adult L01 fraction problem from the entry module to complete the first version, the F1 misconception feedback, and the F2 time-reduced revision. Use paper and pencil or offline documents only; do not recruit real students, charge fees, record other people, or diagnose learning disabilities from this.
What kind of person suits tutors?

Observe whether the person can explain knowledge accurately, hear the reasoning behind an error, give prompts that do not over-answer for the learner, and record actual evidence of their work. Subject knowledge, teaching patience, scheduling, and compliance conditions need to be considered together.

This is editorial career exploration, not a teaching qualification, an organizational permit, or an assessment of real teaching results. One simulated exercise cannot prove long-term learning progress, and it cannot replace employer training or actual position review.

Positive signals are a willingness to verify answers, let learners state their reasoning, adjust questions based on feedback, and admit what they have not yet mastered. Progress records are specific, the language is respectful, and the person is willing to maintain the confidentiality boundaries of learning materials.

Caution signals are doing the homework for the learner, explaining errors with humiliation or labels, promising a guaranteed score increase, or ignoring rules for tutoring minors. When comparing income, also ask clearly about paid teaching hours, preparation, cancellation, and settlement conditions.

Compare the changes across the three versions of the plan, questions, and prompts, check the simulated results on two independent exit problems, and then state what still needs practice. Use a verifiable process to judge whether the person is willing to keep doing teaching support.

The identity for this occupation is tutors, O*NET25-3041.00, providing academic learning support to individuals or small groups. Elementary school teachers, adult basic education teachers, self-improvement course teachers, and university teaching assistants each have their own scope of duties and are not interchangeable just because all of them teach.

Work inputs include course objectives, teaching materials, existing work, the learner's explanation, available time, and the teaching arrangement. First confirm what is to be understood this time, and distinguish an observed error from an unproven cause of the error.

The editorial suggestion is to listen to the explanation first, then verify the knowledge and objectives, choose examples and prompts, and arrange independent work. An error may have many causes, so keep asking rather than attaching labels such as careless, lazy, or learning disability.

Outputs include tutoring plans, practice materials, explanations and feedback, and learning progress records. A correct answer is only part of it, and you also need to observe whether the learner can explain and transfer the idea independently; one performance does not equal long-term mastery.

Individual tutoring can adjust its pace to one learner's reasoning, while small-group tutoring requires attention to different starting levels, participation opportunities, and time allocation at the same time. Online and offline conditions differ, and platform, material, and communication permissions must be verified separately.

Coordinate with the learner and, where applicable, teachers, parents, or program leads. Base feedback on the facts of the work and clarify the next step; share materials only under lawful authorization, and do not treat one conversation as permission to make learning records public.

The typical US BLS entry education for this occupation is some college but no degree, with related experience and on-the-job training classified as none; actual employer conditions vary. This is a US statistical classification and cannot be used to assume that China requires no knowledge, qualifications, or pre-job training.

Keep the objectives, dates, problems, work, and plan revisions, and state what is not yet understood. Use only fictional or lawfully authorized materials in a portfolio; do not freely make learning progress, contact details, or identity information public.

One-on-one misconception tutoring and small-group review support share knowledge verification, questioning, feedback, and recording. The following flow is an editorial summary, not a uniform curriculum or a standard that guarantees learning results.
One-on-one misconception tutoring
Verify objectives and work → listen to the explanation → choose examples and prompts → independent practice → check results → adjust the follow-up plan
Explanations, practice, and progress records for the difficulty being understood this time
Small-group review and learning support
Verify the course and group members' starting levels → plan shared objectives → allocate discussion and practice → check individual understanding → record differences → collect follow-up questions
Group activity materials, individual understanding records, and review arrangements
Shared teaching foundation
Subject knowledge · listening and questioning · learning strategies · feedback adjustment · material confidentiality · compliance conditions
How do one-on-one and small-group tutoring differ? Objectives, process, and responsibility

One-on-one tutoring can more easily adjust prompts around an individual's errors, while groups must balance shared objectives with differences in participation. Both should verify knowledge, let learners work independently, and record real evidence; whether Chinese out-of-school tutoring regulation applies must be verified by the learner group and the actual content.
Core purpose
Provide subject support for one learner's difficulty in understanding, helping them explain their reasoning and gradually complete tasks independently.
Organize review around shared course objectives while identifying each learner's understanding and follow-up needs.
Main subject and basis
Course objectives, teaching materials, one learner's work and explanation, time, and the confirmed teaching arrangement.
Course materials, group members' starting levels, shared difficulties, participation conditions, and the activity scope set by the person in charge.
Core process
Listen and verify the misconception, choose examples, questions, and prompts, gradually withdraw support, then check understanding with independent work.
Explain objectives, organize discussion and practice, allocate participation opportunities, check understanding individually, and adjust follow-up support.
Main outputs
Tutoring plans, practice targeting the misconception, feedback on the work, and specific progress records.
Group review materials, activity records, individual question lists, and follow-up arrangements.
Responsible party

The tutor is responsible for accurate knowledge and feedback and for respecting task and material boundaries; teachers or the organization are responsible for curriculum, assessment, and management according to the actual division of work. A tutor cannot diagnose learning disabilities on their own or promise admission.

The tutor organizes activities and records differences in understanding, and the program lead confirms the curriculum arrangement; group average performance cannot replace evidence of each individual's mastery.
How to coordinate
Confirm with the learner whether you understand their reasoning, clarify with specific questions, and report unresolved points to the applicable teacher or person in charge.
Coordinate the discussion order and practice time, avoid focusing only on the most vocal participants, and refer cases that need extra support according to the program's arrangements.
Delivery boundaries
Providing prompts and explanations does not mean submitting homework, taking exams, or completing tasks for the learner that they should do themselves.
One review session does not guarantee that everyone has mastered the material, and it does not replace formal courses, legal practitioner requirements, or long-term learning assessment.
Key occupational judgments

Judgments must be grounded in course objectives, the learner's explanation, and independent work. Below is the editorially designed work self-check; when qualifications, fees, and material handling are involved, the actual jurisdiction, organization, and authorization must also be verified.
What is the learning objective this time, and do the problems and explanations match it?
What error was observed, and how does the learner explain their own approach?
Do the current examples and prompts help understanding rather than simply giving the homework answer?
After receiving feedback, which teaching assumption and step need to be revised?

Clarify “I don't get it” into specific steps. On this page, F1 points out that the difficulty is converting different denominators to a common unit, so the revision should focus on that difficulty rather than repeating the same-denominator rule the learner already knows.
Are the learning materials, communication methods, and actual training scope approved?

Verify the learner's age, the course, the organization, and material permissions separately. An adult paper simulation does not constitute permission to tutor minors, and private materials must not be given to AI or made public without authorization.
How should independent work results and follow-up needs be retained?

Objective check | Course and learner status | Check the teaching materials and existing work, listen to the learner's explanation, and clarify the objective for this time and the causes that remain unknown.

Material preparation | Examples and practice | Choose materials that fit the objective and starting level, verify answers and difficulty, and avoid content with unclear copyright or unsuited to the grade level.
Teaching support | Explanation and prompts | Use questions, examples, and feedback to support understanding, gradually withdraw support, and protect independent work and academic integrity.
Learning strategies | Methods and plans | Support learning strategies such as reading, note-taking, review, and exam preparation, and adjust the plan with objectives and feedback.

Progress records | Results and communication | Record the problems, the work, and what still needs practice, communicate with the applicable teacher, parent, or person in charge, and do not promise a guaranteed score increase.
Organizational coordination | Time and confidentiality | Arrange tutoring times, coordinate with the relevant people, and store and share learning materials within lawful limits.
Section title | The work environment and working methods of tutors

This occupation emphasizes individual or small-group academic support, ongoing communication, and progress records. The US OOH notes that most work part time, often in the evenings and on weekends, and that demand shifts with the school year and exam schedules; this cannot be extrapolated to uniform working hours in China.

Organization and location | O*NET lists tutoring locations such as homes, libraries, and schools; the OOH also covers online and offline settings. Locations may appear in the occupational tasks, but this does not mean the US wage survey includes tutors hired directly by private households.

Materials and tools | Teaching materials, problems, study plans, records, and communication tools form the work inputs. The exploration on this page can be done with pen and paper, and whether to use a teaching platform or AI depends on the actual organization, material permissions, and content quality.

Work can be organized around individual appointments or program arrangements, and the specific preparation, training, cancelled sessions, and paid time are verified against the actual agreement. Historical campus samples carry enrolled-student restrictions and cannot be treated as full-time community positions.

Scheduling and intensity | Most US tutors work part time, with some evening and weekend work. Teaching hours, preparation, and school-year arrangements for specific Chinese positions must be verified; shorter class time does not mean all the labor is paid.

Communication centers on the specific objective, the work, and the next step, listening to the learner's explanation and giving respectful feedback. Small-group tutoring requires distributing participation opportunities, and humiliation or comparative labels must not replace teaching.

Review and responsibility | The tutor verifies knowledge, answers, and feedback; the organization, teacher, or program lead confirms curriculum and assessment according to the division of work. Out-of-school tutoring for minors in China requires separate verification of approval, category, and practitioner requirements.

Quality requirements | Accurate knowledge, clear objectives, questions suited to the starting level, feedback that can be acted on, progress backed by work evidence, and confidential records. Whether the work looks neat cannot replace real understanding and teaching competence.

The BLS OOH for this occupation, 2025 wages, and the 2025—2035 employment projection; scope, period, and units are each preserved.

Historical campus tutoring recruitment at Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Shenzhen Technology University, supporting specific identity, capability, and pay disclosures; it does not represent nationwide full-time requirements.

China's measures on penalties for out-of-school tutoring and the measures for managing organizational practitioners: verify the applicable scope by learner age, course category, and organizational conditions.
The specific US math tutoring experiment with Tutor CoPilot and the general NIST risk framework: learning results, tool risks, and occupational employment projections each have their own boundaries.

Tutors provide academic support to individuals or small groups, assisting with formal courses or exam preparation. The work includes verifying objectives, preparing materials, listening to explanations, providing prompts, checking independent work, and recording progress; the course, learner, and actual organization determine the working conditions and applicable requirements.
Adult basic education, adult secondary education, and teaching English as a second language, helping adults or out-of-school youth develop basic academic and language skills.
Classroom teaching of the elementary curriculum, arranging instruction and learning assessment, and carrying school position duties.
Teaching non-degree courses aimed at personal interest and self-improvement; whether an actual course involves Chinese non-academic tutoring must be verified separately.
Assisting with teaching support tasks such as material preparation, discussion, exams, and grading under the guidance of a university instructor.

Organize discussion and practice around shared course objectives, and record understanding and follow-up needs separately.
A task direction within this occupation that must account for differences in participation; group average performance cannot replace evidence of individual understanding.
Try designing a division of work and independent checks for the same objective; a real classroom requires carrying this out according to the organization's arrangements and qualifications.
Adult basic education, adult secondary education, English as a second language
The adjacent occupation 25-3011.00 teaches basic education, language, or equivalency courses to adults and others; tutoring in this occupation mainly supports existing courses and exam preparation.
If you would rather design ongoing basic education courses, verify the target position's curriculum, appointment, and adult teaching requirements separately.
Elementary school teachers
The adjacent occupation 25-2021.00 carries out elementary classroom teaching; tutoring experience does not automatically convert into school appointment qualifications.

If you like classroom teaching and ongoing curriculum responsibility, verify school recruitment, teaching qualifications, and practicum requirements, then produce the corresponding teaching materials.
Self-improvement course teachers

The adjacent occupation 25-3021.00 focuses on leisure and self-improvement, usually not for the purpose of earning a degree or occupational qualification; the Chinese training category must be judged by the actual course content.
If you care more about interest-based courses, choose specific content and verify professional capability and teaching rules, rather than judging permits by the job title alone.
University teaching assistants

The adjacent occupation 25-9044.00 assists university instructors with teaching support, with the work constrained by course and supervision arrangements, and does not automatically become an independent course leader.

If you care more about university teaching collaboration, verify student status, course background, and school conditions; a campus peer tutoring sample also does not automatically equal a teaching assistant position.
How do tutors and adjacent teaching occupations differ?

First compare the learners, teaching objectives, actual outputs, and scope of responsibility. In the table below, two entries are task directions within this occupation and four are adjacent occupations with their own O*NET codes; do not assume identical qualifications just because all of them teach.

If you like helping individuals untangle misconceptions, start with the paper tutoring exercise on this page; if you prefer ongoing classroom or basic education courses, verify elementary or adult education positions instead. Interest courses and university teaching assistants also have their own real tasks and entry conditions.

This occupation and the four adjacent occupations are compared using their corresponding O*NET definitions. US occupational classification is used to distinguish tasks and cannot directly establish Chinese certificates, organizational permits, or hiring conditions.

After choosing a direction, use that direction's specific teaching outputs to verify your interest and foundation, then verify the learner group, organizational requirements, and real recruitment conditions.

Task exposure means that some preparation, explanation, or recording steps can be supported by tools, which does not mean the entire tutoring position is replaced. This page has no nationally comparable exposure score for this occupation, and an employment loss probability cannot be calculated from the number of tasks.

One-on-one prompts, group materials, and progress records have different tool uses. The following is an editorial task analysis; applicability must be verified against the learner's starting level, the organization, material permissions, and independent work arrangements.

Real adoption requires organizational or usage survey evidence. Tool access in the specific Tutor CoPilot experiment is not a nationwide adoption rate; this page has no nationally comparable adoption rate for this occupation in China, and prevalence cannot be inferred from software features.

To judge human-machine division of work, first verify the teaching objective, content accuracy, the learner's explanation, and the material scope. Generated prompts can be a reference for the tutor, but they cannot judge the level of understanding, protect rights, or confirm compliance conditions on the tutor's behalf.

The O*NET tasks for this occupation include learning strategies, material preparation, progress monitoring, and communication; the possibility that tools could support these steps is a task-based editorial analysis, not a report by that source of AI time savings or replacement percentages.

Insufficient evidence: there is still no national AI adoption rate, comparable time saving, or independent AI employment causal figure for this occupation in China. Learning results, tool adoption, and employment effects are different subjects, and a 4 percentage point learning result or an overall employment projection cannot be used to fill them in.

First be able to verify knowledge, design questions, and check work independently, then learn to review tool drafts under real organizational rules. Not knowing a particular piece of software does not automatically remove teaching qualifications, and using a tool does not automatically prove teaching competence.

Employment effects require distinguishing replacement, demand, service scale, and other factors. The US BLS projection for this occupation discusses how AI may reduce some demand, but the overall projection is not an independent AI contribution and cannot be extrapolated directly to a layoff rate in China.

Tutor CoPilot randomly assigned tool access to tutors, and both groups had human tutoring; the probability of mastering the after-session problems rose by 4 percentage points overall and by 9 percentage points in the subgroup of low-rated tutors. This is not a 4% score increase, random assignment of students, or a replacement experiment without human tutoring.
How does AI change the tasks of tutors?

Tools can be studied for assisting with generating questions, practice, or records, but humans still need to verify the knowledge, learning objectives, and material permissions. The specific math tutoring experiment provides learning result evidence and cannot yield a nationwide adoption rate or a date for teacher replacement.

Below are the task definition, the specific experiment, US future demand, and the general risk framework. Each source answers a different question; improved learning results and a projection of reduced demand for some services can coexist and do not substitute for each other.

Spring 2024, nine schools in one school district in the southern United States, online math tutoring for grades 3—8; the abstract reports about 900 tutors and 1800 learners. Random tool access was at the tutor level.

The experiment ran for two months from late March 2024, both groups had human tutoring, and randomization was at the tutor level rather than the student level. The text lists different stage figures, including 1787 students, 874 tutors, and 782 at launch, and the approximate numbers in the abstract are not the final analysis counts; no significant improvement was found in end-of-year math test scores, and the after-session exit problem results are not extrapolated to long-term achievement or to all of China.
O*NET25-3041.00 definition, materials, learning strategies, progress, and communication tasks for this occupation, updated 2026.

The task list contains no AI adoption, time saving, replacement rate, or employment causal figures. The tool division of work below is an editorial suggestion and does not claim that O*NET ran an experiment.
The BLS OOH outlook for this occupation from 2025 to 2035, discussing future demand mechanisms such as generative AI and the digitization of practice and test materials.
The official source notes that AI may reduce some tutoring demand; overall growth for this occupation is shown as 0% when rounded to whole numbers, and the exact EMP figure is -0.2%.

This is a US occupational outlook and mechanism description, not a randomized AI employment experiment; the entire net change cannot be attributed to AI, and a decline in Chinese fees cannot be assumed.
The BLS EMP 2025—2035 occupational projection for this occupation, 25-3041, retaining one decimal place and the annual average openings.

208.4 thousand → 208.0 thousand, an official net change of -0.5 thousand and -0.2%, with annual average openings of 34.2 thousand including replacements; the base and the net change are each rounded separately.
The employment projection includes many factors, and openings are not net growth; there is no decomposition of an independent AI effect or any personal employment guarantee.
The NIST AI RMF1.0 general risk framework, covering AI use, measurement, and governance.
Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage support defining the scope of use, verifying accuracy and risk, and recording review and adjustments.

The general framework does not provide tutoring-specific effects, certificates, or regulations; on that basis this page offers editorial suggestions such as minimizing materials and having humans verify answers.
Which tutoring tasks can be studied for tool support?

Drafting materials, suggesting questions, and organizing records can serve as candidate uses; actual teaching must be adjusted to the course and the learner. O*NET only supports task identity and does not prove that tools are already widely used or can complete teaching independently.
Is there a randomized experiment related to this occupation?

The Tutor CoPilot v2 study examines specific online math tutoring in the United States, randomly giving tutors tool access, with both groups receiving human tutoring; the probability of mastering the after-session problems rose by 4 percentage points overall, and this is not whole-course achievement or a Chinese effect.
Does generating practice mean tutors can be reduced?

It does not follow. BLS discusses how digitizing practice and test resources may reduce some demand, and Tutor CoPilot studies assistance within human tutoring. Neither type of evidence can directly determine a specific organization's layoffs, an individual's charges, or employment effects in China.
Are there reliable figures for national adoption, time savings, and independent employment effects?
How should you verify answers given by a tool?

First work it out independently and verify the teaching materials, the meaning of the problem, and its difficulty, then check whether the prompt over-answers. The fraction problem reference on this page uses paper-based human verification only; no AI was called for testing, and the simulated example is not written up as a real tool trial.
Which teaching responsibilities should still rest with people?

This page's editorial suggestion is that the tutor confirms objectives, listens to the learner's explanation, decides prompts and follow-up support, and protects materials and academic integrity. Tool suggestions do not automatically acquire the authority of a teacher, organization, or formal assessor.
What should you learn first when just starting out?

First verify subject knowledge and the course, practice listening, questioning, and accurate feedback, then learn tool review within what the actual organization permits. Show your judgment with original or approved materials, and avoid treating one set of prompts as the whole of your teaching ability.

Choosing explanatory examples and practice
Tools can draft multiple examples, which is a candidate use; quality and time savings were not tested on this page.
Humans verify the problem statement, answers, difficulty, and copyright, and keep the version that fits the course.

Listening to the learner's explanation
Tools can suggest follow-up questions, but they cannot determine the cause or a learning disability from one error.
Listen to the person's reasoning first, record evidence and unknowns, and avoid labels and diagnoses.
Teaching questions
Giving prompts rather than answering for the learner
The CoPilot study supports human-machine tutoring strategies in a specific setting; it does not mean automatic prompts work for every problem.
Verify that prompts match the starting level, gradually withdraw support, and check independent work.
Small-group review
Organizing participation and practice
Draft materials can support discussion preparation; this is an editorial analysis, not a nationwide group effectiveness experiment.
Distribute participation opportunities, check understanding individually, and avoid looking only at the vocal participants.
Progress records
Organizing problems and work
Tools can organize records that are permitted as input; summaries may omit or misstate things.
Check item by item against the problems and the original work, and distinguish what was observed from what was inferred.
Follow-up plan
Adjusting objectives based on feedback
A draft can list practice suggestions, but one correct answer does not mean long-term mastery.
Choose tasks based on the specific misconception and follow-up evidence, and do not promise a score increase or admission.

Reporting to the applicable responsible person
A draft can help with wording, but it does not automatically grant permission to share materials or upload them to external services.
Share within lawful limits and organizational rules, and restrict identity information and real student materials.
One-on-one misconception tutoring
Candidate uses are follow-up questions and draft examples; no time-saving test was done on this page.
Verify knowledge, listen to the person's explanation, adjust prompts, and protect independent work.
Small-group review support
Candidate uses are drafts of activities and tiered practice; one output cannot cover every starting level.
Verify differences in participation, individual understanding, and the actual course arrangement.
Campus peer tutoring
A candidate use is organizing approved materials; real program identity and training conditions must still be met.
Verify enrollment and capability requirements, the material scope, and the program lead's arrangements.
Define the purpose
State the course, subject, objectives, and materials; first verify whether the real organization permits it.
Verify knowledge
Independently verify answers and examples, check difficulty and grade level, and do not trust an output that claims to be correct.
Observe the work
Let the learner explain and complete it independently, and record actual evidence and what remains unknown.
Decide the follow-up
Adjust the plan based on understanding and feedback, and refer to the course lead or a professional when necessary.
Recording and protection
Note the material source, human revisions, and sharing scope, and do not disclose student identities or fabricate results.
Wrong answers
The learner may learn an incorrect rule.
Work it out independently, verify the teaching materials and the problem statement, and do not use an erroneous draft.
Grade level mismatch
The prompt difficulty does not match the starting level and hinders understanding.
First verify the learner's existing knowledge, try revising the prompt, and observe independent explanation.
Over-answering
The homework gets finished without understanding, and academic integrity may be harmed.
Control the degree of prompting, and preserve the learner's own reasoning and independent exit problems.
Material leaks
Learning records or identities are improperly uploaded and made public.
Use only fictional or approved minimal materials, and comply with organizational and applicable protection requirements.
Misjudging results
Claiming that one correct answer or an experiment's result guarantees a score increase, admission, or replacement.
Distinguish simulation from real testing and learning results from employment, and do not invent causal claims or nationwide percentages.
Explorers
Start with the adult fictional paper problem and verify answers and feedback independently; there is no need to buy software or recruit students.
Beginning tutors
Verify practitioner conditions with the real organization, and show knowledge, questioning, revisions, and material boundaries.
People with existing experience
Choose one approved small use, record the original draft, the human verification, and specific failures, then decide whether to keep using it.
Course or program leads
Clarify course quality, material permissions, and review responsibility, and do not judge results by output volume alone.

Insufficient evidence: a nationally comparable wage distribution for tutors in China has not been obtained. The National Bureau of Statistics 2025 urban unit data are published by broad industry categories and do not list this occupation separately, and they exclude the self-employed and freelance workers; the two historical campus samples cannot represent the whole country either.

When discussing pay, first verify the course, the learner group, qualifications, and organizational conditions, then verify the pay unit, whether preparation and training are paid, cancelled sessions, payment, and costs. The hourly teaching fee, the price the student pays, and your own net income are not the same quantity.

Total receipts from self-employed services must also separate costs, taxes, and actual paid time; this page does not assume uniform teaching hours, commissions, or a fixed number of working weeks per year. Whether it is lawful to run actual tutoring also cannot be decided by a quote.

This page reviews two historical campus notices from two institutions; only the Shanghai Jiao Tong University academic tutoring talent pool lists 110 yuan per hour, while the Shenzhen Technology University Peer Tutor notice lists no amount. Both carry enrollment, course, or capability restrictions and cannot be combined into a wage sample for the full-time community market.

The Shanghai Jiao Tong University notice dated 2025-12-18 lists no closing date, and whether recruitment continues now has not been verified. The Shenzhen Technology University item is historical recruitment for a 2024—2025 program. Neither is treated as a verified current opening, and undisclosed guaranteed hours and tax treatment remain unknown.
Tutoring income in China: reading historical campus pay and the national gap separately

Historical notice from the Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Computer Science dated 2025-12-18: tutoring pay of 110 yuan per hour, limited to the school's student talent pool and subject to review; guaranteed hours, tax treatment, and annual income are not disclosed and cannot be annualized.

Historical recruitment for Peer Tutors at the Shenzhen Technology University Writing Center in 2024—2025: eligible students may apply for work-study and receive a monthly payment, with the amount undisclosed; it cannot be assumed that every tutor is paid, nor can the other school's hourly rate be applied.

The Shanghai Jiao Tong University sample is aimed at undergraduate, master's, and doctoral students in the school, requires an overall grade above 90 in the course to be tutored, and lists an hourly rate without guaranteeing assignments; it is not a community part-time job open to anyone.

The Shenzhen Technology University sample is aimed at 2022/2023 cohort Peer Tutors and requires evidence of writing ability and a training assessment, with at least one slot of no less than 2 hours each week; work-study eligibility and the amount must be verified separately.

Comparing quotes also requires verifying whether preparation, training, cancellations, and settlement are paid. Conditions not disclosed in the notice cannot be filled in as confirmed benefits, after-tax income, or annual teaching hours.

The two historical campus programs are not a national probability sample. Without coverage, comparable paid hours, and an income distribution, no national median or uniform high-low pay threshold can be given for this occupation.

A higher hourly rate does not mean tutoring assignments will continue. Record confirmed teaching hours, preparation, and payment separately from unknown arrangements; calendar time or scheduling requirements cannot be used to infer guaranteed paid hours.

Technological change cannot be converted directly into a pay cut for this occupation in China. Tutor CoPilot tests learning results in a specific US math tutoring setting, and BLS discusses US future demand mechanisms; neither provides Chinese individual hourly fee changes, a national adoption rate, or an independent AI employment causal estimate. Specific pay still requires verifying the course, real paid arrangements, and the contract.

Keep the notice date, campus identity, and scope of amount disclosure. The wage gap is not filled in with US statistics, average education industry wages, or the other school's price; historical programs are not written up as verified current recruitment.

The 2025 US median wage for this occupation is 43350 US dollars per year and 20.84 US dollars per hour, from the BLS2025 national wages listed by O*NET. Both units are statistical values, not an individual's annual take-home income or a Chinese tutoring quote.
P10 is 29430 US dollars per year and 14.15 US dollars per hour, describing a lower percentile of US employee wages; it is not an entry level, a starting base pay, or a minimum guarantee.

P90 is 75990 US dollars per year and 36.53 US dollars per hour, a high percentile of US wages; it does not mean someone will certainly reach it, and it does not guarantee paid work throughout the year.

The US EMP2025—2035 projection for this occupation is -0.2%, while the OOH shows 0% as a whole-number percentage; these are not two different projections. The annual average of 34200 openings includes replacement needs and does not mean the same number of net new positions each year.

OEWS wages exclude the self-employed, business owners, and private household employees. The fact that occupational tasks can take place in homes does not mean tutors hired directly by private households are included in the wage survey; the populations for the employment projection and the wage statistics also differ.

OEWS typically forms statistical annual wages on the basis of 2080 standard hours, and this page keeps the official annual and hourly values; this statistical conversion must not be taken as an individual's actual paid time. Part-time work, preparation, and cancelled sessions affect personal income.

values: E1 prompt | adult L01 fraction comprehension

The fictional L01 is a 19-year-old university learner whose goal this time is to understand the common unit for different denominators and fraction addition. Existing work: 1/2+1/3=2/5. Here only the wrong method is known, not the cause, and no diagnosis can be made.

First 20-minute version for reference: ①4 minutes asking “what unit do the two denominators represent?”; expect to hear the learner's own explanation, and since the cause is unknown, feedback restates first without labels. ②6 minutes asking “when the same whole is in six equal parts, how many parts are in one half and in one third?”; expect 3/6 and 2/6, and check that they add to 5/6; if wrong, return to the same whole. ③6 minutes asking “how do you write 2/3 in sixths, and then add 1/6?”; expect 4/6+1/6=5/6, gradually withdrawing prompts. ④4 minutes for the learner to do two exit problems independently with no prompts; expect Q1 to be 3/4 and Q2 to be 5/6, verify each problem in feedback, and do not declare long-term mastery. 4+6+6+4=20.
E2 task | handle F1 and F2 in order

F1: L01 says “I can add with the same denominator, but I am stuck on converting different denominators to the same unit”. Revise the 20-minute version from the first draft: ①4 minutes asking “are you stuck at the step of converting units?”; expect confirmation or further explanation, and verify the difficulty first. ②6 minutes asking “why can one half and one third not be combined directly, and how many sixths is each?”; expect that the units differ, and 3/6 and 2/6; the feedback checks the same whole. ③6 minutes asking “how many 1/6 are in 2/3?”; expect 4, then add 1 more to get 5/6; if wrong, return to the common unit, and if right, withdraw the prompt. ④4 minutes for the same two exit problems done independently, expecting 3/4 and 5/6, verified problem by problem. Change the focus of the follow-up questions and examples, and do not repeat the rule the learner already knows; 4+6+6+4=20.

F2 builds on the F1 version and shortens 20 minutes to 12, with the objective and the two independent exit problems unchanged: ①3 minutes following up on F1 to confirm the difficulty, expecting the learner's own explanation, and recording first if it is unclear. ②4 minutes following the same-whole six-equal-parts question from F1, expecting 3/6, 2/6, and 5/6, with feedback checking the conversion. ③3 minutes following F1 to ask how many 1/6 are in 2/3, expecting 4 plus 1 more, gradually withdrawing prompts. ④2 minutes for the independent exit problems, expecting 3/4 and 5/6 with no prompts, then problem-by-problem feedback. 3+4+3+2=12, compressing discussion and repeated practice without removing the independent check; record truthfully if it is not actually finished.
Reference answers and simulated progress
Common unit reference: 1/2=3/6 and 1/3=2/6, so 1/2+1/3=5/6; 2/3=4/6, and adding 1/6 gives 5/6. The sixths are all based on the same whole, and the denominators are not added.

Exit problems: Q1, 1/4+1/2, standard 3/4; Q2, 2/3+1/6, standard 5/6. The prompt provides simulated responses: L01 Q1 answers 3/4, and Q2 answers 3/9, so one of the two problems is right and one is wrong. Feedback: Q2 did not complete the common-unit conversion correctly, and whether the denominators were added directly still needs to be heard from the learner; next, ask them to explain how 2/3 is written in sixths before practicing new problems. There was no real teaching trial, so no claim of mastery or improvement.
